bib.title: A survey on concept drift adaptation

legacy_report: SOURCE: "A Survey on Concept Drift Adaptation", Joao Gama, Indre Zliobaite, Albert Bifet, Mykola Pechenizkiy, Abdelhamid Bouchachia. ACM Computing Surveys. The file is the author's pre-publication version. Its footer reads "ACM Computing Surveys, Vol. 1, No. 1, Article 1, Publication date: January 2013", with placeholder DOI "10.1145/0000000.0000000" and "35 pages". The PDF does NOT confirm the 2014 volume, issue or DOI. The "2014" in the filename and any ACM CSUR 46(4) citation would have to be checked outside this file. COVERAGE: 44 pages, 155,981 chars (pypdf; my re-extraction counted 157,600, probably a newline difference). I read the body (survey, sections 1-5), the online appendix (pseudocode, datasets, MOA example) and the Figure 11 and 12 text. The reference list (lines ~1558-1873) was only skimmed for origins. Text was clean. Figures were not rendered, and only their captions and surrounding text were read. The Fig 12 numbers are not in the text. CLAIMS (ranked) - Drift is defined as a change in the joint distribution, and drift types are split by which component changes. Only real drift changes p(y|X) and requires adaptation. number: none setup: supervised online learning, general definition quote: "concept drift between time pointt0 and time pointt1 can be deﬁned as ∃X :pt0(X,y )⁄=pt1(X,y )" and "From a predictive perspective only the changes that affect the prediction decision require adaptation." where: sec 2.1, pp 3-4 - Taxonomy of drift types: real (p(y|X) changes, with or without a p(X) change), virtual (p(X) changes only), population drift, and prior-probability drift. The paper notes that "virtual drift" has several meanings in the literature and fixes its own. quote: "Real concept drift refers to changes inp(y|X)." and "In this paper virtual drift refers to change in the data distributionp(X)." where: p 4 - Drift patterns over time: sudden/abrupt, incremental, gradual, reoccurring, and outliers (outliers are not drift). Drift can also be characterised by severity, predictability and frequency. A detector must not confuse noise or outliers with drift. quote: "One of the challenges for concept drift handling algorithms is not to mix the true drift with an outlier or noise" where: sec 2.2, p 5 (Fig 2) - Requirements for models in changing environments, and the generic adaptive loop of predict, diagnose, update. The four modules are Memory, Change Detection, Learning, Loss Estimation. Labels may be delayed or absent. quote: "(1) detect to concept drift (and adapt if needed) as soon as possible; (2) distinguish drifts from noise and be adaptive to changes, but robust to noise; (3) operate in less than example arrival time and use not more than a ﬁxed amount of memory" where: sec 2.3-2.4, pp 6-7 (Fig 3) - Four families of change detection (Fig 6, sec 3.2): (i) sequential analysis (SPRT, CUSUM, Page-Hinkley); (ii) control charts / SPC (and EWMA); (iii) monitoring two distributions on two windows (ADWIN, Kifer, KL divergence, entropy, paired learners); (iv) contextual (Splice, IFCS). The survey states the trade-off between the families. quote: "comparing two distributions for change detection requires more computational resources than detecting based on the evolution of indicators, but potentially may give more precise information about the location of change." where: p 18 - Cost of each detector family (Table II): sequential analysis and SPC are O(1) memory and time. Two-distribution monitoring (ADWIN) is O(logW) to O(W). number: O(1); O(logW)-O(W) quote: "sequential analysis O(1) O(1) CUSUM, PH ... monitoring two distributions O(logW )−O(W ) O(logW )−O(W ) ADWIN" where: Table II, p 18 - SPC / DDM rule with three states, based on the Bernoulli/Binomial error rate. Warning is p_i+s_i >= p_min+2*s_min (about 95% confidence). Out-of-Control is >= p_min+3*s_min (about 99%). It needs n > 30 examples. The time between Warning and Out-of-Control measures the rate of drift. In Algorithm 3, the instances buffered during Warning are used to train the new model after Out-of-Control. number: 2 sigma / 3 sigma; n>30; 95% / 99% quote: "A commonly used conﬁdence level for Warning is 95% with the threshold pi +σi≥ pmin + 2∗σmin, and for Out-of-Control is 99% with the thresholdpi +σi≥pmin + 3∗σmin." where: sec 3.2.2, p 16 - CUSUM: g_t = max(0, g_{t-1} + (x_t - delta)), alarm if g_t > lambda, then reset to 0. Page-Hinkley: m_T is the cumulative deviation from the mean minus delta, M_T is its running minimum, and an alarm fires when PH_T = m_T - M_T > lambda. Trade-off: low delta means faster detection but more false alarms. Larger lambda means fewer false alarms but possibly missed changes. CUSUM is memoryless, and its accuracy depends on delta and lambda. quote: "Low values of δ allow faster detection, at the cost of increasing the number of false alarms." and "Larger λ will entail fewer false alarms, but might miss some changes." where: sec 3.2.1, p 15 - EWMA: Z_t = (1-lambda)Z_{t-1} + lambda*e_t. It signals when Z_t > mu_0 + L*sigma_Zt, where L is the control limit. quote: "We can signal a change when Zt > µ0 +LσZt." where: p 16 - ADWIN: two sub-windows are compared with a Hoeffding-bound cut, and the older sub-window is dropped when the means differ. It assumes no data distribution. Default confidence delta suggested is 0.2. Memory and time are O(log W) per item thanks to an exponential histogram. number: eps_cut = sqrt((1/2m) ln(4|W|/delta)); delta default 0.2; O(logW) quote: "δ is a user deﬁned conﬁdence parameter, the suggested default value is 0.2." and "it stores this data in onlyO(logW ) memory andO(logW ) processing time per item, rather than theO(W )." where: p 17 - Detection by comparing a fixed reference window to a sliding recent window with a statistical test (null hypothesis that the distributions are equal), per Kifer et al. 2004 and KL-divergence methods (Dasu 2006, Sebastiao & Gama 2007). Detection windows are conceptually different from training windows. quote: "If the null hypothesis is rejected, a change is declared at the start of the recent window." where: sec 3.2.3, p 16 - Adaptation strategies, blind vs informed. Blind adaptation (fixed windows, example weighting, incremental learners such as VFDT) forgets at a constant speed and is slow to react. Informed adaptation (triggered by a detector) can replace the model globally or locally (CVFDT grows an alternate subtree). quote: "The blind approaches forget old concepts at a constant speed independently of whether changes are happening or not." where: sec 3.3.2, p 20 - Memory taxonomy: data management (single example vs multiple examples/windows, fixed or variable size) and forgetting (abrupt: sliding or landmark windows, reservoir sampling; gradual: fading factor alpha, exponential weights w=exp(-lambda*j)). Window-size trade-off: short window is fast but noisy, long window is stable but slow. Recency assumption fails with noise, reoccurring concepts, or slow drift longer than the window. quote: "A short window reﬂects the current distribution more accurately, thus it can assure fast adaptation in periods with concept changes, but in stable periods too short window worsens the performance of the system." where: sec 3.1, pp 11-13 - Ensembles are grouped into dynamic combination, continuous update, and structural update. Methods named: SEA (fixed-size ensemble, drops worst member), DWM (weights multiplied by beta on mistakes, new expert added when the ensemble errs, prune below theta), AddExp, Learn++.NSE, Wang et al. 2003 (weights = MSE_r - MSE_i), DDD (low- and high-diversity ensembles). Diversity finding from Minku et al. 2010: quote: "before the drift occurs, ensembles with less diversity obtain lower test errors, but shortly after the drift occurs, highly diverse ensembles are better regardless the type of drift." where: sec 3.3.3, pp 21-23 - Reoccurring concepts: FLORA3 was first. Store old models in a sleeping mode and select among them by meta-learning (Gama & Kosina 2011). where: p 23 - Loss estimation without a holdout: compare a short-window (or small fading factor) error estimate to a long-term one, and run Page-Hinkley on their ratio (Gama et al. 2013). Fading factors were somewhat faster than sliding windows in the authors' report. quote: "Their experiments show that drift detection based on the ratio of fading estimates is somewhat faster that with sliding windows." where: sec 3.4, p 24 - Evaluation protocol for streams. Cross-validation is not applicable because it mixes temporal order. Use holdout, prequential (interleaved test-then-train) with landmark window, sliding window or fading factor, and controlled permutations (Zliobaite 2011b) for order bias. Averaging accuracy over time can hide adaptation behaviour. quote: "cross-validation is not directly applicable to the streaming settings with evolving data because it would mix the temporal order of data." where: sec 4.2, pp 26-27 - Metrics for the detector itself: probability of true detection, probability of false alarms (best expressed as average run length, evaluated only on drift-free data), detection delay, and detection point accuracy. Streaming cost metrics: RAM-Hours (1 GB for 1 hour) and Kappa statistic for imbalance. quote: "we may use the inverse of the time to detection or the average run length , the expected time between false positive detections" where: sec 4.1, pp 25-26 - Significance testing: McNemar statistic M = sign(a-b)(a-b)^2/(a+b), rejects equal performance when M > 6.635 at 0.99 confidence. Nemenyi test with CD = q_alpha*sqrt(k(k+1)/6N) after Friedman, for more than two classifiers. number: 6.635 quote: "At 0.99 conﬁdence it rejects the null hypothesis (the performances are equal) ifM >6.635." where: sec 4.2.3, p 28 - MOA demo (only empirical result): a stream of one million instances from the Random RBF generator with centroid drift speed 1e-4 per instance, scored prequentially with a window of 1000. The sliding-window prequential estimate closely approximates holdout. Hoeffding Tree adapts worst. Ensembles do better but cost more RAM-Hours. Leveraging Bagging has the highest accuracy and Kappa and the highest resource use. number: 1,000,000 instances; speed 10^-4; window 1000. No accuracy values are given in the text. quote: "Hoeffding Tree is the method with lower capacity of adaption. Ensemble methods perform better than single classiﬁers, but they have a higher cost in RAM-Hours." where: App C, App-8 - Application categories: monitoring and control, management and strategic planning, personal assistance and information, ubiquitous environments. Examples: boiler mass flow, wind power with online training, spam, Netflix, and the DARPA Stanley car. Competition winners credited modelling temporal dynamics. quote: "it is important ﬁrst to understand the nature and source of drift and only then engineer an effective adaptive learning strategy." where: sec 2.5, p 10 - Benchmark datasets. Synthetic: SEA (thresholds theta = 9, 8, 7, 9.5), STAGGER, rotating hyperplane, RBF, function generator, LED (Bayes accuracy 74%), waveform (86%). Real: ELEC2 electricity (45,312 instances), ECUE spam (>10,000 emails over ~2 years), PAKDD'09 credit (5 years), Airline (~116M records). quote: "The ELEC2 dataset contains 45, 312 in-stances." where: App B, App-3 to App-6 LIMITS - The scope is online supervised learning with real drift. The paper says it excludes drift detectable from p(X) alone, tracking drifting priors, novelty detection, and clustering-based semi-supervised methods. It points to other work for those. This is the opposite emphasis from input-feature and data-quality monitors, which are label-free. - Labels are assumed to arrive promptly. The paper concedes that feedback may be delayed, biased, costly or absent, and that validation for delayed or unsupervised settings "only start to be investigated". - It concedes a closed-loop or reinforcement-feedback bias: "we cannot evaluate and compare the performance of concept drift handling techniques by replaying historical data." - Open challenges listed: scalability, robustness, interpretable and explainable adaptation, less dependence on labels, adaptive systems that automate the whole knowledge-discovery pipeline, and integrating expert knowledge. - No head-to-head benchmark across detectors. The one experiment is a single MOA illustration. Synthetic data is noted as uncertain to reflect real drift. - Dated: 2013 text, so it has no deep-learning drift work, no feature-store or ML-platform monitoring practice, and no unsupervised multivariate tests such as MMD or PSI as practised today. BUILDS ON (as printed) Page 1954 (CUSUM, Page-Hinkley); Wald 1947 (SPRT); Basseville and Nikiforov 1993; Schlimmer and Granger 1986 (STAGGER, origin of the term concept drift); Widmer and Kubat 1993 and 1996 (FLORA); Gama et al. 2004 (SPC drift detection); Bifet and Gavalda 2006 and 2007 (ADWIN); Kifer et al. 2004; Domingos and Hulten 2000 (VFDT); Hulten et al. 2001 (CVFDT); Street and Kim 2001 (SEA); Kolter and Maloof 2003 and 2007 (DWM); Littlestone 1987 (Winnow); Tsymbal 2004 (prior survey); Gao et al. 2007 and Kelly et al. 1999 (drift decomposition); Moreno-Torres et al. 2012 (dataset shift); Zliobaite 2011b; Gama et al. 2013 (fading-factor loss estimation); Vitter 1985 (reservoir sampling); Bifet et al. 2011b (MOA).
